Relational Archival Investigation: Identity, Chronology, and Historical Judgment in Korean Experimental Art
(2026)
Dorian Vale
no media files associated
open exposition
About this exposition
Relational Archival Investigation (RAI) is a source-critical method for determining what relationships among records can establish about the identity, chronology, explanation and historical consequences of artworks. This study compares seven consecutive acquisition entries in the 2016 Annual Report of the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Korea (MMCA), with their public collection descriptions. Two leading production-year assignments differ. Published artist testimony distinguishes production from presentation in one case. The reason for the other difference remains open. Additional comparisons distinguish an early one-monitor presentation from a later twelve-monitor arrangement, a title’s reported origin from its subsequent adoption, and a performance from the later repair of a photograph that records it. Post-Interpretive Criticism provides a philosophical background. The findings rest on a bounded set of Korean experimental art cases and their documented sources.

This exposition brings together the main manuscript and its two separately citable supplements. It uses National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Korea (MMCA, 국립현대미술관) and Seoul Museum of Art Archives (SeMA, 서울시립 미술아카이브) sources to trace work identity, dating, photography, and exhibition history. The cases concern Lee Kang-so (이강소), Park Suk-won (박석원), Sung Neung Kyung (성능경), Kim Youngjin (김영진), Kim Yong-Ik (김용익), Rim Dong Sik (임동식). Dorian Vale, Museum of One, 2026. ORCID 0009-0004-7737-5094.

When Documentation Becomes the Work: Photographs, Reperformance, and the Archival Lives of Korean Experimental Art
(2026)
Dorian Vale
no media files associated
open exposition
About this exposition
Dorian Vale · Museum of One · Working paper · Version 2.0 · 10 November 2026 · 16 pages · 42 references
Canonical DOI:
https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24095308
This working paper compares how photographs acquired artistic and institutional standing through copying, repair, printing, exhibition, collection and reperformance in Korean experimental art. The cases concern Rim Dong Sik (임동식), Kim Kulim (김구림) and Sung Neung Kyung (성능경). This edition adds SeMA’s collection transfer chronology, KADA’s classification and digitization account, the exhibition checklist for video associated with Kim’s reperformance, and Kim Eunjin’s Korean-language conservation study.

Scope and limits. SeMA describes Rim’s copying and repair. Item-level repair and transfer dates remain unresolved. Kim’s source negative, edition, printing authorization, purchase year and recording lineage remain open. MMCA identifies Sung’s collected twelve-print panel with the panel shown in 1976. The manufacture and mounting of individual sheets remain unresolved. Three Korean journal articles were consulted through published abstracts.

RAI overlap. The author’s Relational Archival Investigation working paper and supplements share earlier analyses of Rim’s repair and Sung’s photographic exhibition. Version 2.0 extends the comparison through Kim’s print and reperformance history, the additional institutional records and Korean conservation scholarship.

Titles, Dates, and Reconstructed Works: Four Documentary Histories of Korean Experimental Art
(2026)
Dorian Vale
no media files associated
open exposition
About this exposition
A work can retain its title and historical date even when its materials, arrangement, or means of presentation have changed. This working paper examines four Korean archival and museum cases: Kim Yong-Ik’s Plane Object photographs and the history of “plain” and “place”; the differing production years assigned to Park Suk-won’s Jeok–Eungnyeok; the 1975 historical reference and 2016 materials of Lee Kang-so’s Untitled 75031; and Kim Kulim’s Mediator, used by the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Korea, to exemplify compound dating. MMCA’s acquisition narrative and publication guidance acknowledge remaking as part of collecting an experimental past. The paper reads that institutional practice alongside scholarship on the relations among images, material traces, and artwork identity. Aga Wielocha’s discussion of Danh Vo’s chandeliers provides a particularly revealing comparison: a title can date an object’s removal and transformation into art rather than its fabrication, just as a museum’s leading year can identify an earlier work rather than the age of its present components. These different histories require the event dated by each title or caption to remain explicit. Neither artist authorisation nor institutional recognition settles every claim about an earlier condition. The paper credits the overlapping demonstrations in the author’s Relational Archival Investigation papers and develops their implications for collecting, editorial preference, and historical inference. Its contribution is a comparative account of how names and dates sustain continuity without making the evidence for that continuity interchangeable.

Museum of One working paper · Version 1.0 · 10 November 2026 · 16 pages · 21 references. Canonical DOI:
https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24095953
The case studies compare museum records, contemporaneous criticism, exhibition documentation and artist testimony. Object-specific acquisition and conservation files and the original artworks remain unexamined. Jung Eun Young is cited through the published abstracts. The three cited Relational Archival Investigation (RAI) releases contain overlapping source comparisons and already establish the limitations of shared series titles and conflicting eight- and ten-photograph accounts. This paper adds sustained comparative histories and expanded sources. RAI DOI links:

Answerability: Exhibition, Documentation, and Historical Evidence in Postwar Japanese Art
(2026)
Dorian Vale
no media files associated
open exposition
About this exposition
This working paper develops a claim-specific criterion of historical answerability through engagement with Reiko Tomii’s scholarship on operation in postwar Japanese art. It asks when evidence concerning exhibition, documentation, and artistic organization requires an art-historical account to reconsider the boundary of the work it claims to explain.

The principal case is Shiraga Kazuo’s Challenging Mud. Tomii’s accounts of material preparation and anticipated display are read beside Namiko Kunimoto’s analysis of action, object, agency, and selfhood. Further investigations address press presentation and photographic selection, Hi Red Center and GUN, conditions of authorization, and the differentiation of events and photographic records in museum cataloguing. The comparison does not presume a disagreement between Tomii and Kunimoto or equate evidence of preparation with complete predetermination.

The method distinguishes attribution, justification, and historical accuracy. Before evaluating a challenge, it fixes a proposition’s referent, meaning, scope, certainty, and evidential basis. Retention, limitation, revision, and suspension identify possible consequences of evidence without becoming compulsory stages or an aesthetic scoring system. The analysis separates a supported preparation-display relation from stronger claims about intention and distinguishes documentation’s original public operation from the reach of its later historical testimony.

The contribution is a disciplined account of inferential reach within the historical problems Tomii’s research makes visible. It also refines the application of restraint in Post-Interpretive Criticism: the amount of explanation cannot be prescribed before its evidential function is examined. This is a source-critical study of published arguments, not an independently inspected archival reconstruction or an empirical study of museum audiences. The criterion remains open to further cases and scholarly revision.

After the Interpretation Changes: Correction, Completion, and the Circulation of Museum Titles
(2026)
Dorian Vale
no media files associated
open exposition
About this exposition
This study distinguishes two changes in the Rijksmuseum’s presentation of Simon Maris’s portrait now titled Isabella: the withdrawal of a racialized catalogue title in 2015, and the fulfilment in 2020 of an announced intention to adopt a name when one became known. The second change does not, by itself, demonstrate revision of the rule governing the first. The records examined at Europeana and Wikimedia Commons reveal different afterlives of the later decision. Europeana retains the descriptive title and an account in which identification remains unfinished. Commons preserves the older wording in the name of its image file while identifying the work as Isabella in the accompanying description. Drawing on my correspondence with Alexander V. Markov, the study follows what these descriptions do, rather than treating their survival as evidence of continuing authority. It finds uneven presentation of the later naming decision, not a demonstrated restoration of the rejected title. Its contribution to Post-Interpretive Criticism is a documentary distinction among correction, completion and circulation.

Independently authored by Dorian Vale and published by Museum of One as Research Working Paper No. 2, version 1.0. Developed through scholarly correspondence with Alexander Viktorovich Markov and his subsequent critical response to the documentary study. Selected passages and summaries are reproduced with his permission. Markov is not a coauthor, and the study is not a record of formal peer review or agreement with every proposal. The full private correspondence is not published.

When Interpretation Becomes Authority
(2026)
Dorian Vale
no media files associated
open exposition
About this exposition
A Museum of One research dialogue between Post-Interpretive Criticism (PIC) and the Semiotics of Non-intentional Ephemerality (SNE). Dorian Vale’s editorial account follows a scholarly exchange with Alexander V. Markov (Alexander Viktorovich Markov; Александр Викторович Марков) on how interpretations acquire authority through museum labels, catalogue descriptions, teaching conventions, and search terms. It traces the semantic protocol, successional authority, deactivation gap, recognition closure, and responsibilities of contestability. The account attributes Markov’s intellectual contributions and relates the exchange to Vale’s separate documentary study of the Rijksmuseum’s retitling of Simon Maris’s Isabella. public_item_metadata.title: Relational Archival Investigation: Identity, Chronology, and Historical Judgment in Korean Experimental Art
public_item_metadata.creator: Dorian Vale
public_item_metadata.description:
Relational Archival Investigation (RAI) is a source-critical method for determining what relationships among records can establish about the identity, chronology, explanation and historical consequences of artworks. This study compares seven consecutive acquisition entries in the 2016 Annual Report of the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Korea (MMCA), with their public collection descriptions. Two leading production-year assignments differ. Published artist testimony distinguishes production from presentation in one case. The reason for the other difference remains open. Additional comparisons distinguish an early one-monitor presentation from a later twelve-monitor arrangement, a title’s reported origin from its subsequent adoption, and a performance from the later repair of a photograph that records it. Post-Interpretive Criticism provides a philosophical background. The findings rest on a bounded set of Korean experimental art cases and their documented sources.

This preservation copy contains the research manuscript and its two separately citable companions.

public_item_metadata.title: When Documentation Becomes the Work: Photographs, Reperformance, and the Archival Lives of Korean Experimental Art
public_item_metadata.creator: Dorian Vale
public_item_metadata.description:
Dorian Vale · Museum of One · Working paper · Version 1.0

Canonical DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24093529 · ORCID

Photographs give Korean experimental art a continuing public form through copying, repair, printing, exhibition and collection. This working paper compares Rim Dong Sik’s photographic copies and reported repairs, Kim Kulim’s 1970 action, its 2000 print and 2016 reperformance, and Sung Neung Kyung’s Reading Newspaper, its 1976 photographic exhibition and Event Logical brochure. The comparison distinguishes material continuity, exhibition history and institutional identification as claims that require different evidence.

Artists: Rim Dong Sik (임동식), Kim Kulim (김구림), Sung Neung Kyung (성능경).

한국어 연구 요약 이 작업 논문은 한국 실험미술에서 사진이 복제, 보수, 인화, 전시, 수집을 거치며 작품을 접할 수 있는 공개적 형태가 되는 과정을 비교한다. 서울시립미술관의 기록을 바탕으로 임동식의 퍼포먼스 사진에 가해진 개입을 살피고, 국립현대미술관의 기록을 통해 김구림의 〈현상에서 흔적으로〉가 1970년에 행해진 사건, 2000년에 인화된 소장품, 2016년에 재연된 사건으로 이어지는 경로를 구분한다. 성능경의 〈신문 읽기〉는 1976년 사진 전시와 《Event Logical》 브로슈어를 중심으로 살핀다. 사진의 개별 촬영 시점과 현존 인화물의 제작·처리 이력에는 미해결 문제가 남는다. 이 연구는 전시 이력, 물질적 연속성, 기관의 작품 식별에 각각 어떤 근거가 필요한지 묻는다. 논문 본문은 영어로 제공된다.

Limits of the evidence. SeMA’s descriptions support the attributed account of Rim’s copying and repair. The exact repair date and individual interventions remain unresolved. The negative, edition and print history in Kim’s case remain open. Sung’s individual exposures and the material continuity of the 1976 panel remain unresolved. Three Korean journal articles were consulted through their published abstracts only.

RAI overlap. The author’s Relational Archival Investigation working paper and two technical supplements drew on an earlier draft for Rim’s repair and Sung’s early exhibition. This working paper extends that evidence with Kim’s case, the 1976 brochure accounts, and scholarship on performance, photography and conservation. Related papers: RAI main paper · Documentary supplement · Extended case studies.

© 2026 Dorian Vale · Museum of One. In Copyright.

public_item_metadata.title: Titles, Dates, and Reconstructed Works: Four Documentary Histories of Korean Experimental Art
public_item_metadata.creator: Dorian Vale
public_item_metadata.description:
Working paper · Version 1.0 · Published 10 November 2026 · Dorian Vale · Museum of One. Not independently peer reviewed.

Canonical DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24095953

A work can retain its title and historical date even when its materials, arrangement, or means of presentation have changed. This working paper examines four Korean archival and museum cases: Kim Yong-Ik’s Plane Object photographs and the history of “plain” and “place”; the differing production years assigned to Park Suk-won’s Jeok–Eungnyeok; the 1975 historical reference and 2016 materials of Lee Kang-so’s Untitled 75031; and Kim Kulim’s Mediator, used by the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Korea, to exemplify compound dating. MMCA’s acquisition narrative and publication guidance acknowledge remaking as part of collecting an experimental past. The paper reads that institutional practice alongside scholarship on the relations among images, material traces, and artwork identity. Aga Wielocha’s discussion of Danh Vo’s chandeliers provides a particularly revealing comparison: a title can date an object’s removal and transformation into art rather than its fabrication, just as a museum’s leading year can identify an earlier work rather than the age of its present components. These different histories require the event dated by each title or caption to remain explicit. Neither artist authorisation nor institutional recognition settles every claim about an earlier condition. The paper credits the overlapping demonstrations in the author’s Relational Archival Investigation papers and develops their implications for collecting, editorial preference, and historical inference. Its contribution is a comparative account of how names and dates sustain continuity without making the evidence for that continuity interchangeable.

Limitations: No physical inspection of artworks, original photographic versos, complete 1978 printing proofs, or object-specific acquisition and conservation dossiers was undertaken. No independently dated sequence of MMCA database versions is established for Park Suk-won. A shared series title cannot establish the identity of every individual Kim Yong-Ik work; Lee Kang-so’s eight- and ten-photograph accounts do not establish a sequence of additions. Jung Eun Young (2024) remains abstract-only. Four selected cases do not establish prevalence across Korean museums.

RAI overlap disclosure: This paper develops findings already published in the author’s Relational Archival Investigation (version 1.0, 9 November 2026; DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24088563), Documentary Evidence and Source Comparisons (10.5281/zenodo.24088574), and Extended Case Studies and Methodological Demonstrations (10.5281/zenodo.24088573). These are shared findings, not independent corroboration. The distinct contribution is the sustained comparison of MMCA’s acquisition narrative, compound-date convention, and Mediator, alongside expanded Kim Yong-Ik evidence and the Ryu and Wielocha comparisons.

© 2026 Dorian Vale · Museum of One. In Copyright. English; 16 pages; 21 references.

public_item_metadata.title: Answerability: Exhibition, Documentation, and Historical Evidence in Postwar Japanese Art
public_item_metadata.creator: Dorian Vale
public_item_metadata.description:
This working paper develops a claim-specific criterion of historical answerability through engagement with Reiko Tomii’s scholarship on operation in postwar Japanese art. It asks when evidence concerning exhibition, documentation, and artistic organization requires an art-historical account to reconsider the boundary of the work it claims to explain.

The principal case is Shiraga Kazuo’s Challenging Mud. Tomii’s accounts of material preparation and anticipated display are read beside Namiko Kunimoto’s analysis of action, object, agency, and selfhood. Further investigations address press presentation and photographic selection, Hi Red Center and GUN, conditions of authorization, and the differentiation of events and photographic records in museum cataloguing. The comparison does not presume a disagreement between Tomii and Kunimoto or equate evidence of preparation with complete predetermination.

The method distinguishes attribution, justification, and historical accuracy. Before evaluating a challenge, it fixes a proposition’s referent, meaning, scope, certainty, and evidential basis. Retention, limitation, revision, and suspension identify possible consequences of evidence without becoming compulsory stages or an aesthetic scoring system. The analysis separates a supported preparation-display relation from stronger claims about intention and distinguishes documentation’s original public operation from the reach of its later historical testimony.

The contribution is a disciplined account of inferential reach within the historical problems Tomii’s research makes visible. It also refines the application of restraint in Post-Interpretive Criticism: the amount of explanation cannot be prescribed before its evidential function is examined. This is a source-critical study of published arguments, not an independently inspected archival reconstruction or an empirical study of museum audiences. The criterion remains open to further cases and scholarly revision.

Research Working Paper No. 1. Version 1.0. 10 pages.

Independent working paper by Dorian Vale, developed following discussion and feedback from Reiko Tomii. Tomii is not a coauthor. Her feedback is not represented as endorsement or formal peer review. Private correspondence and meeting records are not reproduced.

Research programme and detailed study overview: https://www.museumofone.art/reiko-tomii/

public_item_metadata.title: After the Interpretation Changes: Correction, Completion, and the Circulation of Museum Titles
public_item_metadata.creator: Dorian Vale
public_item_metadata.description:
This study distinguishes two changes in the Rijksmuseum’s presentation of Simon Maris’s portrait now titled Isabella: the withdrawal of a racialized catalogue title in 2015, and the fulfilment in 2020 of an announced intention to adopt a name when one became known. The second change does not, by itself, demonstrate revision of the rule governing the first. The records examined at Europeana and Wikimedia Commons reveal different afterlives of the later decision. Europeana retains the descriptive title and an account in which identification remains unfinished. Commons preserves the older wording in the name of its image file while identifying the work as Isabella in the accompanying description. Drawing on my correspondence with Alexander V. Markov, the study follows what these descriptions do, rather than treating their survival as evidence of continuing authority. It finds uneven presentation of the later naming decision, not a demonstrated restoration of the rejected title. Its contribution to Post-Interpretive Criticism is a documentary distinction among correction, completion and circulation.

Independently authored by Dorian Vale and published by Museum of One as Research Working Paper No. 2, version 1.0. Developed through scholarly correspondence with Alexander Viktorovich Markov and his subsequent critical response to the documentary study. Selected passages and summaries are reproduced with his permission. Markov is not a coauthor, and the study is not a record of formal peer review or agreement with every proposal. The full private correspondence is not published.

© 2026 Dorian Vale · Museum of One. CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 applies to the author's original contribution. Rights in third-party material and the original correspondence remain with their respective holders. Permission for selected correspondence material does not extend to reproduction of the full exchange.

final_pending_task_review.title: When Documentation Becomes the Work: Photographs, Reperformance, and the Archival Lives of Korean Experimental Art
final_pending_task_review.description:
Dorian Vale · Museum of One · Working paper · Version 1.0

Canonical DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24093529 · ORCID

Photographs give Korean experimental art a continuing public form through copying, repair, printing, exhibition and collection. This working paper compares Rim Dong Sik’s photographic copies and reported repairs, Kim Kulim’s 1970 action, its 2000 print and 2016 reperformance, and Sung Neung Kyung’s Reading Newspaper, its 1976 photographic exhibition and Event Logical brochure. The comparison distinguishes material continuity, exhibition history and institutional identification as claims that require different evidence.

Artists: Rim Dong Sik (임동식), Kim Kulim (김구림), Sung Neung Kyung (성능경).

한국어 연구 요약 이 작업 논문은 한국 실험미술에서 사진이 복제, 보수, 인화, 전시, 수집을 거치며 작품을 접할 수 있는 공개적 형태가 되는 과정을 비교한다. 서울시립미술관의 기록을 바탕으로 임동식의 퍼포먼스 사진에 가해진 개입을 살피고, 국립현대미술관의 기록을 통해 김구림의 〈현상에서 흔적으로〉가 1970년에 행해진 사건, 2000년에 인화된 소장품, 2016년에 재연된 사건으로 이어지는 경로를 구분한다. 성능경의 〈신문 읽기〉는 1976년 사진 전시와 《Event Logical》 브로슈어를 중심으로 살핀다. 사진의 개별 촬영 시점과 현존 인화물의 제작·처리 이력에는 미해결 문제가 남는다. 이 연구는 전시 이력, 물질적 연속성, 기관의 작품 식별에 각각 어떤 근거가 필요한지 묻는다. 논문 본문은 영어로 제공된다.

Limits of the evidence. SeMA’s descriptions support the attributed account of Rim’s copying and repair. The exact repair date and individual interventions remain unresolved. The negative, edition and print history in Kim’s case remain open. Sung’s individual exposures and the material continuity of the 1976 panel remain unresolved. Three Korean journal articles were consulted through their published abstracts only.

RAI overlap. The author’s Relational Archival Investigation working paper and two technical supplements drew on an earlier draft for Rim’s repair and Sung’s early exhibition. This working paper extends that evidence with Kim’s case, the 1976 brochure accounts, and scholarship on performance, photography and conservation. Related papers: RAI main paper · Documentary supplement · Extended case studies.

final_pending_task_review.title: Titles, Dates, and Reconstructed Works: Four Documentary Histories of Korean Experimental Art
final_pending_task_review.description:
Working paper · Version 1.0 · Published 10 November 2026 · Dorian Vale · Museum of One. Not independently peer reviewed.

Canonical DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24095953

A work can retain its title and historical date even when its materials, arrangement, or means of presentation have changed. This working paper examines four Korean archival and museum cases: Kim Yong-Ik’s Plane Object photographs and the history of “plain” and “place”; the differing production years assigned to Park Suk-won’s Jeok–Eungnyeok; the 1975 historical reference and 2016 materials of Lee Kang-so’s Untitled 75031; and Kim Kulim’s Mediator, used by the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Korea, to exemplify compound dating. MMCA’s acquisition narrative and publication guidance acknowledge remaking as part of collecting an experimental past. The paper reads that institutional practice alongside scholarship on the relations among images, material traces, and artwork identity. Aga Wielocha’s discussion of Danh Vo’s chandeliers provides a particularly revealing comparison: a title can date an object’s removal and transformation into art rather than its fabrication, just as a museum’s leading year can identify an earlier work rather than the age of its present components. These different histories require the event dated by each title or caption to remain explicit. Neither artist authorisation nor institutional recognition settles every claim about an earlier condition. The paper credits the overlapping demonstrations in the author’s Relational Archival Investigation papers and develops their implications for collecting, editorial preference, and historical inference. Its contribution is a comparative account of how names and dates sustain continuity without making the evidence for that continuity interchangeable.

Limitations: No physical inspection of artworks, original photographic versos, complete 1978 printing proofs, or object-specific acquisition and conservation dossiers was undertaken. No independently dated sequence of MMCA database versions is established for Park Suk-won. A shared series title cannot establish the identity of every individual Kim Yong-Ik work; Lee Kang-so’s eight- and ten-photograph accounts do not establish a sequence of additions. Jung Eun Young (2024) remains abstract-only. Four selected cases do not establish prevalence across Korean museums.

RAI overlap disclosure: This paper develops findings already published in the author’s Relational Archival Investigation (version 1.0, 9 November 2026; DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24088563), Documentary Evidence and Source Comparisons (10.5281/zenodo.24088574), and Extended Case Studies and Methodological Demonstrations (10.5281/zenodo.24088573). These are shared findings, not independent corroboration. The distinct contribution is the sustained comparison of MMCA’s acquisition narrative, compound-date convention, and Mediator, alongside expanded Kim Yong-Ik evidence and the Ryu and Wielocha comparisons.

final_pending_task_review.title: When Interpretation Becomes Authority
final_pending_task_review.description: A Museum of One research dialogue between Post-Interpretive Criticism (PIC) and the Semiotics of Non-intentional Ephemerality (SNE). Dorian Vale’s editorial account follows a scholarly exchange with Alexander V. Markov (Alexander Viktorovich Markov; Александр Викторович Марков) on how interpretations acquire authority through museum labels, catalogue descriptions, teaching conventions, and search terms. It traces the semantic protocol, successional authority, deactivation gap, recognition closure, and responsibilities of contestability. The account attributes Markov’s intellectual contributions and relates the exchange to Vale’s separate documentary study of the Rijksmuseum’s retitling of Simon Maris’s Isabella.
